findings.antecedent: Lamp type A (3500K, 2330lm) vs. Lamp type D (5000K, 2330lm)
findings.mechanism: The SEL method predicted higher brightness for D, but similar brightness was observed, indicating a failure of the SEL method.
findings.quote: Lamps A and D were rated as providing similar spatial brightness, even though lamp type D had higher CCT than A.

findings.consequent: belief: 'Bright, harsh fluorescent lighting can make me feel tense' (LB9)
findings.mechanism: Participants' attitudes changed, showing increased agreement with this statement after experiencing different lighting conditions.
findings.quote: The attitudes on three questions (i.e., LB9, LB23, LB24) changed significantly after the study

findings.consequent: belief: 'I like to have more light when I am working on a computer' (LB23)
findings.mechanism: Participants' attitudes changed, showing decreased agreement with this statement after experiencing different lighting conditions.
findings.quote: The attitudes on three questions (i.e., LB9, LB23, LB24) changed significantly after the study

findings.consequent: belief: 'If the light is visually cool, my office environment feels uncomfortable' (LB24)
findings.mechanism: Participants' attitudes changed, showing increased agreement with this statement after experiencing different lighting conditions, consistent with negative ratings for 5000K CCT.
findings.quote: The attitudes on three questions (i.e., LB9, LB23, LB24) changed significantly after the study

stimuli.description: Office spaces (open-plan, cubicles, private offices, common areas, conference rooms) with fluorescent lighting manipulated for CCT and lumen output. Four lamp types (3500K/2330lm, 5000K/2935lm, 3500K/3000lm, 5000K/2330lm) were used.

tables.description: Index of the four treatment conditions (lamp types A, B, C, D) with corresponding nominal CCT and lumen output, and S/P ratios.
Summary of EMA questions and mean responses by participants under each treatment condition, separated by daylight access.
Summary of web-based survey questions and mean responses by participants under each treatment condition, separated by daylight access.
Summary of lighting belief questions included in the first and last web-based surveys, with mean, median, std. dev. before and after, and p-values for paired t-test.
Mean illuminances (lx) and standard deviations in three private offices under different lamp types.
Statistical significance for the effects in linear mixed-models for the questions included in the EMAs and web-based surveys.
key_stats: p-values for CCT, Daylight, Lumen, and their interactions across various dependent variables, all <0.001 or <0.05

limitations: The study was a field study, making it impractical to counterbalance the order of the four lamp types to avoid potential order bias.
The pre-post method of data collection (web-based surveys) is limited by recall bias.
The sample size of 26 participants is relatively small, though the number of responses for EMAs and web-based surveys is larger due to repeated measures.
